blocks.title: 1. The Range
teacherCues: Ask: 'What is the simplest way to describe how spread out a set of numbers is?'
Write the formula: Range = Maximum – Minimum.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: A small range does not necessarily mean the data are reliable or accurate. [[imp:Always consider the context and look for outliers before interpreting the range.]]

hints: Range is small but doesn't show that most scores are 9s and 10s; a more detailed measure like standard deviation would be better.
challengeCorner.prompt: A teacher recorded quiz scores: 8, 9, 10, 10, 10, 9, 8, 7, 10, 6. Find the range. Is the range a good measure of consistency here?

examples.prompt: Find the range of these temperatures: 32°F, 45°F, 50°F, 68°F, 72°F, 40°F.
examples.title: A – Compute the range

steps: The range only considers the two most extreme values.
If one value is an outlier, the range will be large even if the rest of the data are clustered together.
It ignores the distribution of the middle values.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about a data set with one extreme outlier.
examples.title: B – Why range isn't enough
examples.prompt: Explain why the range alone can be misleading about the variability of a data set.

steps: The outlier drastically inflates the range.
examples.title: C – Range with outlier
examples.prompt: A company's daily sales last week were \$800, \$820, \$790, \$810, \$2,500 (a special bulk order). Find the range with and without the outlier.

discoveryHook.scenario: Two classes took the same test. Class A scores range from 60 to 100 (range = 40), while Class B scores range from 80 to 90 (range = 10). Although both classes might have the same average, Class A's scores are much more spread out. The [[kw:range]] gives a quick measure of variability.

questions.prompt: If all values in a data set are identical, the range is ___ (number).

formulaCard.title: Range
notes: Easy to compute, but sensitive to extreme values.
Often used as a preliminary measure before more detailed analysis.

explanation: The [[kw:range]] is the difference between the largest and smallest values in a data set.
$$\text{Range} = \text{Maximum Value} - \text{Minimum Value}$$
It is the simplest measure of dispersion, but it only uses two values and can be greatly affected by outliers.
A larger range indicates more variability; a smaller range indicates the data are closer together.
[[imp:The range does not tell us anything about the distribution of values between the extremes.]]

visuals.caption: Both classes might have similar means, but Class A has a much larger range.
visuals.title: Comparing Ranges of Two Classes

teacherCues: Ask: 'How can we measure the average distance of each data point from the mean?'
Introduce standard deviation as a more comprehensive measure of spread.

discoveryHook.scenario: Two investment funds have the same average annual return of 8%. Fund A's returns over 5 years were 6%, 7%, 8%, 9%, 10%. Fund B's returns were 0%, 5%, 8%, 11%, 16%. Fund B's returns are much more volatile. The [[kw:standard deviation]] quantifies this volatility—it's a measure of how far the data points are from the mean.

rows.1: Find the mean ($\bar{x}$) of the data.
For each value, compute the deviation from the mean ($x_i - \bar{x}$).
Divide by (n – 1) for sample standard deviation.
Take the square root of the result.

visuals.caption: The formula uses squared deviations to eliminate negative signs and emphasize larger deviations.
visuals.title: Steps to Calculate Sample Standard Deviation

explanation: The [[kw:standard deviation]] measures the average distance of each data point from the mean. It is the most common measure of dispersion.
For a population: $$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}}$$ where $\mu$ is the population mean and $N$ is the population size.
For a sample (more common in business): $$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}$$ where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean and $n$ is the sample size.
A larger standard deviation means more variability; a smaller one means the data are more tightly clustered around the mean.
[[imp:Standard deviation is always non‑negative; it is zero only if all values are identical.]]

formulaCard.title: Standard Deviation Formulas
notes: Use $n-1$ for samples to get an unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation.
The standard deviation has the same units as the original data.

confusionCorner.body: When calculating by hand, use the sample formula with $n-1$ unless you know the data represent the entire population. [[imp:Most business data are samples.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

challengeCorner.prompt: Compute the sample standard deviation of these five test scores: 70, 80, 85, 90, 100.

examples.title: A – Compute standard deviation (small sample)
examples.prompt: Find the sample standard deviation of: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9.

examples.peerPrompt: What happens when you sum the raw deviations?
examples.title: B – Why square the deviations?
examples.prompt: Explain why we square the deviations before summing, instead of just averaging the raw deviations.
steps: The sum of raw deviations from the mean is always zero (positive and negative cancel).
Squaring makes all values positive, so they don't cancel.
It also gives more weight to larger deviations, which better reflects variability.

examples.prompt: Find the sample standard deviation of: 10, 12, 23, 23, 16, 23, 21, 16.
examples.title: C – Practice standard deviation

blocks.title: 2. Standard Deviation – Concept and Formula

questions.prompt: Standard deviation measures the average distance of data points from the ___.
In the sample standard deviation formula, the denominator is n – ___ (number).

teacherCues: Explain that for bell‑shaped (normal) distributions, about 68% of data lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD, and 99.7% within 3 SD.
Use the life expectancy example from the chapter opener.

challengeCorner.prompt: The average height of adult males is 70 inches with a standard deviation of 3 inches. If heights are normally distributed, what is the approximate percentage of males taller than 76 inches?
hints: 95% are within ±2 SD, so 5% outside. Half (2.5%) above +2 SD.

formulaCard.title: Empirical Rule
notes: Can be used to detect outliers: values beyond ±3 SD are very unusual.

explanation: The [[kw:empirical rule]] (68–95–99.7 rule) applies to data that are approximately bell‑shaped and symmetric.
About 68% of data fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean: $\mu \pm 1\sigma$.
About 95% within 2 standard deviations: $\mu \pm 2\sigma$.
About 99.7% within 3 standard deviations: $\mu \pm 3\sigma$.
This rule helps us understand how unusual a particular data point is.
[[imp:These percentages are approximate; they work best for large data sets that follow a normal distribution.]]

visuals.title: Empirical Rule (Mean = 100, SD = 15)
visuals.caption: This is why IQ scores with mean 100 and SD 15 classify 95% of people between 70 and 130.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The empirical rule applies only to normal distributions. [[imp:If the data are skewed, these percentages do not hold.]]

questions.prompt: For a normal distribution, about ___% of data lie within one standard deviation of the mean.
Mean = 200, SD = 25. The 95% interval is ___ to ___ (numbers only, no comma, e.g., 150 250).
A value that is 3 standard deviations above the mean is considered ___ (word: unusual or typical).

examples.title: A – Apply empirical rule
examples.prompt: A company's employee salaries are normally distributed with mean \$50{,}000 and standard deviation \$5{,}000. About 95% of employees earn between what two amounts?

steps: Compute z = (75,000 – 50,000) / 5,000 = 5. So it's 5 standard deviations above the mean.
The empirical rule says only 0.3% of data are beyond ±3 SD.
A salary 5 SD above the mean is extremely unusual—an outlier.
examples.title: B – Detecting an outlier
examples.peerPrompt: Think about how many standard deviations above the mean it is.
examples.prompt: Explain how you would use the empirical rule to decide if a salary of \$75{,}000 is unusually high for this company.

examples.title: C – Percent within 1 SD
examples.prompt: If a factory's output weights are normally distributed with mean 100 grams and SD 8 grams, what percent of products weigh between 92 and 108 grams?
steps: By the empirical rule, about 68% are within 1 SD.
So about 68% weigh between 92 and 108 grams.

discoveryHook.scenario: The chapter opener states that life expectancy has a standard deviation of 10 years. If the mean life expectancy is 76.4 years, then about 68% of people live between 66.4 and 86.4 years (mean ± 1 SD), and 95% live between 56.4 and 96.4 years. This is the [[kw:empirical rule]] for normally distributed data.

blocks.title: 3. Interpreting Standard Deviation (Empirical Rule)

questions.prompt: A lower CV indicates ___ consistency. (word: more or less)

blocks.title: 4. Comparing Variability with Coefficient of Variation

hints: Fund A has higher CV, so relatively riskier.
challengeCorner.prompt: Fund A has mean return 12\%, SD 3\%. Fund B has mean return 9\%, SD 1.8\%. Compute CV for both and determine which is relatively riskier.

confusionCorner.body: CV is not meaningful when the mean is zero or negative. [[imp:Use only for ratio‑level data with positive means.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

visuals.title: Comparing Variability with CV
visuals.caption: Even though Store B has a smaller SD, its relative variability is higher.

formulaCard.title: Coefficient of Variation
notes: CV is useful when comparing volatility of investments (risk per unit of return).
CV should not be used when the mean is near zero.

explanation: The [[kw:coefficient of variation (CV)]] expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean.
$$\text{CV} = \frac{\text{Standard Deviation}}{\text{Mean}} \times 100$$
It is a relative measure of dispersion, useful for comparing variability between data sets with different units or different means.
A lower CV indicates more consistency (less variability relative to the mean).
[[imp:CV is unitless, making it ideal for comparisons across different types of data.]]

teacherCues: Ask: 'How can we compare the consistency of two data sets with different means?'
Introduce the coefficient of variation (CV) = (SD / Mean) × 100.

discoveryHook.scenario: A pizza delivery chain wants to compare delivery times of two stores. Store A has mean 20 minutes, SD 4 minutes. Store B has mean 12 minutes, SD 3 minutes. Store A's standard deviation is larger, but is it actually less consistent relative to its mean? The [[kw:coefficient of variation]] (CV) = (SD / Mean) × 100: A's CV = 20%, B's CV = 25%, so Store B is relatively more variable.

examples.prompt: Investment X has average return 10\% with SD 2\%. Investment Y: average return 8\% with SD 1\%. Which is relatively riskier?
examples.title: A – Compute CV
steps: Investment X has higher relative risk.

examples.title: B – Why use CV?
steps: SD measures absolute variability, but a higher SD might be acceptable if the return is proportionally higher.
CV scales the SD by the mean, showing risk per unit of return.
This gives a fair comparison even when means are very different.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about what happens when one investment has a much higher return.
examples.prompt: Explain why CV is better than SD for comparing risk across different investments.
Machine 1 produces bolts with mean length 50 mm, SD 0.5 mm. Machine 2: mean length 30 mm, SD 0.4 mm. Which is more consistent?
examples.title: C – Production consistency

Work through a problem that asks for range, standard deviation, and interpretation.
blocks.title: 5. Blueprint Aid for Measures of Dispersion

discoveryHook.scenario: A quality control manager measures the diameters of 10 ball bearings (in mm): 5.1, 5.0, 4.9, 5.2, 5.0, 5.1, 4.8, 5.2, 5.1, 5.0. Use the blueprint to calculate the range, standard deviation, and CV, and determine if the process is consistent.

questions.prompt: The first step of the blueprint is to ___ the data.
Data: 4, 8, 6, 10. Mean = 7. Sum of squared deviations = ___ (number only).
In the final step, you should ___ your result in the context of the problem. (word)

hints: Mean=305/6≈50.83; range=55-48=7. Deviations squared sum≈30.84, variance=6.168, sd≈2.48, CV=4.88%.
Low CV indicates consistent battery life.
challengeCorner.prompt: A sample of 6 batteries lasted (hours): 48, 52, 55, 50, 49, 51. Compute the mean, range, standard deviation, and CV. Is the battery life consistent?

confusionCorner.body: Always compute the mean to one more decimal place than the original data when calculating standard deviation to reduce rounding error. [[imp:Round only the final answer.]]
confusionCorner.title: Watch out!

notes: If the problem states the data are a population, use N instead of n-1.
Always check for outliers before interpreting the standard deviation.
formulaCard.title: Dispersion Blueprint

explanation: Apply the blueprint to dispersion problems:
1. Understand: list the data, determine if it's a sample or population, and note what measures are needed.
2. Solve: compute the mean, range, deviations, squared deviations, variance, standard deviation, and CV if useful.
3. Conclude: interpret the standard deviation in context; use the empirical rule if the distribution is normal; compare CV to benchmarks.
This structured approach ensures you don't skip steps in the standard deviation calculation.

visuals.title: Blueprint: Ball Bearing Diameters
visuals.caption: Follow the steps carefully; small data sets are sensitive to rounding.

rows.1: Compute deviations, square, sum, divide by 9, sqrt.
Low CV indicates very consistent production.

examples.prompt: Explain how the blueprint helps you avoid common mistakes like forgetting to square the deviations or dividing by n instead of n-1.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about the order of steps.
steps: The 'Solve' step explicitly lists squaring the deviations and dividing by (n-1).
It reminds you to take the square root at the end.
